ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
An ideal transformer has a turns ratio between its primary and secondary coils of $n_{1}:n_{2}=5:1$. The primary coil is connected to a sinusoidal alternating power supply with a peak voltage of $U_{m}$. The secondary coil is connected to a heating wire with resistance $R$. The heating wire is sealed inside an adiabatic container, which encloses a certain mass of ideal gas. Before heating begins, the gas temperature is $T_{0}$.

1. Determine the output power $P$ of the transformer.
2. Given that the heat $Q$ absorbed by the gas in the container is directly proportional to its temperature change $\Delta T$, expressed as $Q=C\Delta T$, where $C$ is a known constant. Assuming all the heat generated by the heating wire is absorbed by the gas, calculate the time $t$ for which the heating wire needs to be energized to double the gas pressure inside the container.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is the primary coil of a transformer connected to a sinusoidal AC power supply, labeled n_1; on the right side is the secondary coil, labeled n_2. The upper end of the secondary coil passes through switch S and then is connected to the resistance wire R inside the rectangular container on the right, the resistance wire is located inside the container, and the circuit then returns to the lower end of the secondary coil. Reasoning: It is known that the turns ratio of the ideal transformer is n_1:n_2=5:1, and the peak value of the AC voltage connected to the primary coil is U_m. The effective value of the sinusoidal voltage is U_1=U_m/\sqrt{2}. For an ideal transformer, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, so the effective voltage of the secondary coil is U_2=(n_2/n_1)U_1=U_m/(5\sqrt{2}). The resistance of the resistance wire is R, therefore the output power is P=U_2^2/R=U_m^2/(50R). The container is sealed and its volume is unchanged, and the gas is a certain mass of ideal gas, so p\propto T. To double the pressure, the temperature needs to change from T_0 to 2T_0, therefore \Delta T=T_0. The heat absorbed by the gas is Q=C\Delta T=CT_0. All the heat generated by the resistance wire is absorbed by the gas, hence Pt=Q, so t=Q/P=CT_0/(U_m^2/(50R))=50CT_0R/U_m^2.
